edges.note: Operates without prejudice to Regulation (EU) 2016/679; FRIA under Article 27 integrates with GDPR Article 35 DPIA.
High-risk AI systems complying with CRA essential cybersecurity requirements are presumed compliant with AI Act Article 15 cybersecurity duties.
Aligned with Council of Europe Framework Convention on AI (CETS 225), formally concluded by the EU in 2026.
Article 9 Risk Management and Article 55 GPAI systemic risk evaluations parallel NIST AI RMF 1.0 and AI 600-1.
Profiling (Art. 4(4)), biometric data (Art. 9), automated decision-making (Art. 22), and DPIAs (Art. 35) anchor EU AI Act Article 6(3), Article 10(5), and Article 27.
Products with digital elements that are also high-risk AI systems enjoy presumption of conformity with AI Act Article 15 when CRA essential cybersecurity requirements are satisfied.
CRA governs product-level security and ENISA single-reporting-platform notifications, complementing NIS2 entity-level obligations.
DORA operates as lex specialis for financial entities regarding ICT risk management and incident reporting.
Supply chain cybersecurity and 24-hour early warning incident reporting align with CRA vulnerability handling.
Overrides NIS2 entity-level ICT risk and incident reporting for regulated EU financial institutions.
First legally binding international AI treaty; formally approved/concluded by the European Union in mid-2026.
Reinforces UNGA human-rights lifecycle protection norms.
Contrasts with the 2024/2025 UN Hanoi Cybercrime Convention through stricter Article 15 human-rights, proportionality, and judicial oversight conditions.
Global UN treaty covering ICT-enabled offenses and cross-border electronic evidence sharing for serious crimes; requires 40 ratifications to enter into force.
Affirms full applicability of IHL (Geneva Conventions and Additional Protocol I Arts. 35, 36, 48, 51, 57) to all autonomous weapons systems.
Global consensus baseline paired with Independent International Scientific Panel on AI.
Primary binding IHL benchmark for military AI, autonomous targeting, and cyber warfare.
Maps to EU AI Act Article 9 Risk Management and Article 55 systemic risk evaluations.
NIST AI RMF compliance functions as an explicit affirmative defense or safe-harbor benchmark in US state AI statutes (e.g., Colorado AI Act).
Primary source of binding statutory AI obligations in the United States following federal EO 14110 revocation.
Mirrors EU AI Act structural themes (prohibited manipulations, high-risk discrimination duties, frontier training-data/safety disclosures) under state Attorney General enforcement.
Mandatory explicit and implicit synthetic content labeling effective Sept 1, 2025 predates EU AI Act Article 50 enforcement (Aug 2, 2026).
Completes full verbatim 1949 Geneva Convention coverage alongside Geneva Convention IV and Additional Protocol I.
Affirmed by ICJ as embodying intransgressible principles of customary international humanitarian law.
Develops and supplements Common Article 3 for Non-International Armed Conflicts (NIAC), prohibiting attacks on civilians and terrorizing civilian populations.
UK Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 reforms automated decision-making rules relative to EU GDPR Article 22 and CJEU SCHUFA.
Sectoral principles-based regulatory model contrasted with EU AI Act horizontal risk tiers.
World's first dedicated national governance standard specifically targeting tool-calling autonomous AI agents.
Maps agentic permissions, least-privilege sandboxing, and kill-switch governance onto AIMS controls.
Asia's first comprehensive binding AI statute (effective Jan 22, 2026), paralleling EU AI Act high-risk and transparency regimes with extraterritorial domestic-agent requirements.
Risk management and impact assessment rules interoperate with ISO/IEC 42001 controls.
Rejects EU-style upfront administrative fines in favor of AI Strategy Headquarters oversight, mandatory misuse-investigation cooperation, and public naming powers.
Latin America's flagship EU-inspired AI bill; approved by Federal Senate Dec 10, 2024 and pending Chamber of Deputies Special Committee (PL233823) vote.
Provides certifiable management-system architecture aligned with EU AI Act Article 17 QMS and Article 9 Risk Management.
Explicitly recognized alongside NIST AI RMF as a rebuttable presumption of reasonable care in US state AI legislation.
Direct structural crosswalk between ISO 42001 Clauses 4-10 / Annex A and NIST AI RMF 1.0.
Holds that automated probability/credit scoring strongly relied upon by a downstream lender is itself a 'decision based solely on automated processing' under GDPR Article 22(1).
Directly governs creditworthiness AI systems classified as high-risk under EU AI Act Annex III.
Invalidated EU-US Privacy Shield and mandated Transfer Impact Assessments and supplementary safeguards for international AI/cloud data transfers under SCCs.
Restricts reliance on contractual necessity or legitimate interest for off-platform AI behavioral profiling and confirms competition authorities may examine GDPR breaches.
Defines strict EU Charter proportionality boundaries for automated real-time algorithmic analysis of electronic communications metadata and national security retention.
Constrains indiscriminate surveillance while permitting targeted cyber-threat retention subject to independent judicial review.

Establishes that distinction and unnecessary suffering are 'intransgressible principles of international customary law' and that IHL applies to all future weapons technologies (foundational precedent for LAWS reviews).
Primary ICJ authority cited in UN CCW GGE LAWS deliberations confirming IHL covers novel autonomous weapons.
